title: Tibetan teachers in exile
hook: after 1959 Tibetan teachers settle in India, then teach worldwide

segments.voice: Yesterday: temples in the West, and services held inside a fence. Your line: kept their ground.

A high mountain pass, snow to the knees, thin air. A monk walks it with a bundle tied to his back: a few long, loose-leaf texts wrapped in cloth, the kind we saw in the Tibetan canons. Behind him are the monasteries where he learned to read them. Ahead, the foothills of India, a country he has never seen. When the Dalai Lama left Tibet for India, monks, nuns, teachers and families followed him over passes like this one, on foot.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN PASS.` → `TEXTS TIED TO HIS BACK.` → `INTO INDIA.`

segments.voice: The Dalai Lama settled in Dharamsala, a hill town in the north of India, and it became the center of Tibetan life in exile, with its own offices, schools, temples and a library for Tibetan texts. Monks who made it across rebuilt their great monasteries in settlements in southern India, on farmland far from the snow. Sera, Drepung and Ganden, names from the hills around Lhasa, rose again there, and the debate courtyards came back too: monks clapping and questioning each other in the afternoon, as they had at home. In exile, teachers met students from everywhere. Lamas from the Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug schools traveled to Europe, North America, Asia and beyond, and founded centers where people who had never seen Tibet learned its chants, meditations and texts. A refugee may have to leave almost everything behind. These teachers carried the teaching in memory, in practice, and in those loose-leaf texts on their backs. In the last year of the Buddha's life, as Rhys Davids' translation of the Book of the Great Decease tells it, he gave this advice to Ananda: "be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." A refuge you can carry. For teachers who lost their monasteries, their country and their road home, that is what the teaching had to become, and what they handed on to students they could never have pictured meeting.
screen: `A HOME IN DHARAMSALA.` · `MONASTERIES REBUILT IN INDIA.` · `TEACHERS GO OUT INTO THE WORLD.` · `A REFUGE YOU CAN CARRY.` · then, large: `TEACHING IN EXILE.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one person who had to leave home: someone you know, someone in your own family's story, a face from the news, or a monk on a mountain pass. Think of what they had to leave and what they managed to carry, and if you like, silently wish them safety and a place to rest. Then let the picture go, and sit.
Dharamsala. The hill town in India where the Dalai Lama settled and Tibetan teachers rebuilt their monasteries and taught the world.
Your line: teaching in exile. Be a lamp, be a refuge, wherever the road goes. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep up their monasteries, schools and debate in India and Nepal, and Tibetan teachers lead centers around the world where students study and practice in their lineages.

They kept it secret, teaching only Tibetans, until they could go back home.
They left the old texts behind and made up a new, simpler teaching instead.

notes: Editor: fixed the garbled line 'a refugee can leave almost everything behind' and varied the practice opening, which repeated yesterday's 'Bring one to mind. It might be'.
Claims rule: the index hook says 'after 1959'; no year is spoken. The exile is placed 'when the Dalai Lama left Tibet for India'. Confirm.
Dharamsala as the center of exile life, with offices, schools, temples and a library (the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives): confirm wording.
Sera, Drepung and Ganden re-founded in settlements in southern India (Bylakuppe and Mundgod): confirm.
Four schools named without a count; confirm that naming them this way is fair (Bon and Jonang are not named).
Rhys Davids quotation reused from earlier in the path (DN 16); confirm wording and section number.

Audit: the lamp-and-refuge advice is given to Ananda during the illness at Beluva, months before the final days, so 'in the Buddha's last days' and 'to his followers' became 'in the last year of the Buddha's life' and 'to Ananda' (teach and myth).
A sensitive political subject: the script describes the exile without assigning blame or stating politics. A Keeper may want a short neutral cause added or not.
